---
title: "Study B: quality check before analysis"
format: html
---

Before we ask Study B (the contraception cohort) any biological question, we
check the data itself. If a sample is mislabelled or a count file is broken,
every later result inherits the mistake silently, so we spend one report on
this first.

Each of the checks below is small on purpose: load, ask one question, print
`PASS` or `FLAG`. Nothing here drops samples or edits data — we only decide
what to *watch out for* when the analysis documents come.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
# The workshop helper: reads all six Study B files and puts them in one list.
source(here::here("R/count_tables.R"))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ggplot2))

d <- read_counts("group_b")   # one item per file, plus $path

# A tiny helper: prints PASS or FLAG so every check is easy to skim.
check <- function(ok, what) {
  cat(if (isTRUE(all(ok))) "PASS " else "FLAG ", what, "\n", sep = "")
}
```

## 1. What the study looks like

The metadata file (`01_metadata.csv`) has one row per sample. Let's see how
many people there are, which arm they are in, and whether the two sequencing
batches are balanced across arms — if one arm were mostly batch B1 we could not
tell arm effects from batch effects later.

```{r}
#| label: design
meta <- d$metadata

cat("samples:", nrow(meta),
    " unique participants:", n_distinct(meta$participant_id), "\n\n")

table(meta$arm)
table(meta$arm, meta$rnaseq_batch)   # arm (rows) x batch (columns)
table(meta$arm, meta$bv)             # BV status (Nugent-based) per arm
```

```{r}
#| label: design-ranges
# Ranges of the numeric columns: Nugent score is 0-10, vaginal pH ~3.5-6.
summary(meta |> select(nugent, ph))
table(meta$any_sti)

check(!any(is.na(meta)), "no missing values in the metadata")
```

**What we learned:** 93 people, one sample each, three arms (injectable 39,
pill 28, ring 26). The two sequencing batches are almost perfectly balanced
across arms, which is what we want. No missing values anywhere in the
metadata.

## 2. Do the six files agree? (the most important check)

Both count tables have **features in rows, samples in columns**. Almost every
tool we will use matches the count table's column 1 to the metadata's row 1
*by position*, without checking names. If the orders ever differed, nothing
would warn us — results would just be wrong. So we check it explicitly.

```{r}
#| label: order
check(identical(colnames(d$species), meta$sample_id),
      "microbiome columns match metadata rows, in the same order")
check(identical(colnames(d$genes), meta$sample_id),
      "rnaseq columns match metadata rows, in the same order")
check(identical(d$cytokines$sample_id, meta$sample_id),
      "cytokine rows match metadata rows, in the same order")
check(!any(duplicated(meta$sample_id)), "no duplicate sample IDs")

# Internal consistency: the bv column should agree with the Nugent score,
# which is what it was derived from (>= 7 is the usual cut-off for positive).
check(all((meta$nugent >= 7) == (meta$bv == "positive")),
      "bv label agrees with the Nugent >= 7 cut-off for every sample")
```

All five pass, so we can use any of the tables without re-ordering.

## 3. Microbiome counts

Counts must be whole numbers (you cannot sequence 0.5 of a read) and never
negative. We also look at **library size** — the total counts per sample, i.e.
how deeply that sample was sequenced. Very shallow samples give noisy
estimates and are the usual reason to exclude a sample.

```{r}
#| label: micro-qc
sp <- d$species

check(all(sp == round(sp)), "species counts are whole numbers")
check(all(sp >= 0),       "no negative counts")
check(!any(is.na(sp)),    "no missing values")

cat("features (species):", nrow(sp), " samples:", ncol(sp), "\n")
```

```{r}
#| label: micro-depth
# Library size = column sums: total counts assigned to that sample.
depth <- tibble(
  sample_id = colnames(sp),
  reads     = colSums(sp),
  arm       = meta$arm,
  batch     = meta$rnaseq_batch
)
summary(depth$reads)

ggplot(depth, aes(arm, reads)) +
  geom_col() +                              # one bar per sample
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Microbiome sequencing depth, per sample",
       subtitle = "One bar per person",
       x = NULL, y = "Total counts per sample")
```

```{r}
#| label: micro-depth-flags
shallow <- depth |> filter(reads < 10000) |> arrange(reads)
shallow

check(nrow(shallow) == 0, "no sample below 10,000 counts (a shallow-sample cut-off)")

# How many species were never seen at all?
zero_species <- sum(rowSums(sp) == 0)
check(zero_species < nrow(sp) / 2,
      paste("fewer than half the species rows are all-zero (actual:", zero_species, "of", nrow(sp), ")"))

# The species we do see should look like a vaginal community:
# Lactobacillus is usually the most abundant genus.
rel <- sweep(sp, 2, colSums(sp), "/")       # each sample's counts / its total
lac <- grepl("lactobacillus", rownames(rel), ignore.case = TRUE)
cat("median Lactobacillus share per sample:", round(median(colSums(rel[lac, ])), 2), "\n")
```

**What we learned:** the table is clean (whole numbers, no negatives, no
NAs), but it is sparse — 86 of the 220 species are **never observed in any
sample**, and 88% of the cells are zero. That is normal for this kind of data
but it means the "features in rows" table carries a lot of dead weight.
One sample, `r shallow$sample_id[1]`, is shallow (`r format(shallow$reads[1], big.mark = ",")` counts vs a median around 29,000) — worth remembering, though not bad enough to act on. Lactobacillus (mostly *L. iners* and *L. crispatus*) dominates the median sample, as expected for this body site.

## 4. RNAseq counts

Same checks, plus one specific to this table: every gene in the count table
should also be in the annotation file (`05_gene_annotation.csv`), otherwise we
cannot name what we find.

```{r}
#| label: rna-qc
gn <- d$genes

check(all(gn == round(gn)), "gene counts are whole numbers")
check(all(gn >= 0),        "no negative counts")
check(!any(is.na(gn)),     "no missing values")

check(setequal(rownames(gn), d$gene_info$ensembl_gene_id),
      "count table and annotation contain exactly the same genes")

missing_symbol <- d$gene_info |> filter(is.na(symbol) | symbol == "")
cat("genes in counts:", nrow(gn),
    " genes missing a symbol:", nrow(missing_symbol), "\n")

gdepth <- tibble(
  sample_id = colnames(gn),
  reads     = colSums(gn),
  batch     = meta$rnaseq_batch
)
summary(gdepth$reads)

ggplot(gdepth, aes(batch, reads)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "RNA sequencing depth, per sample",
       x = "Sequencing batch", y = "Total counts per sample")

cat("genes detected per sample (nonzero):",
    min(colSums(gn > 0)), "to", max(colSums(gn > 0)), "\n")
```

**What we learned:** the gene table matches its annotation exactly (14,226
genes in both), and no sample looks failed — every sample has 12,000+ genes
detected. Twenty-four genes have no symbol; the helper handles that by using
their Ensembl ID as the name, so nothing is lost. Depth is lower in batch B2
than B1 (median about 12.0M vs 13.7M) — mild, but batch is worth including in
any model we fit.

## 5. Cytokines

```{r}
#| label: cyto-qc
cy <- d$cytokines
na_per_sample <- rowSums(is.na(cy[, -1]))

cy |> filter(na_per_sample > 0) |> select(sample_id, il1b, il6, tnfa)
check(all(na_per_sample %in% c(0, ncol(cy) - 1)),
      "each sample has either all 15 cytokines or none (no half-failed samples)")

# Cytokines are measurements, not counts, so we only check plausibility.
vals <- unlist(cy[, -1])
check(all(vals[!is.na(vals)] >= 0), "no negative concentrations")
```

**What we learned:** two samples, `B018` and `B029`, have **no cytokine values
at all** — the assay simply failed for them. They are fine in the count tables,
so we keep them everywhere except any cytokine analysis, which should either
drop those two rows or let the model handle the missingness.

## 6. Verdict

The data are in good shape. Summary of what to carry forward:

| Flag | What | What to do about it |
|---|---|---|
| OK | Sample IDs agree across all six files, in order | Use tables as loaded, no re-ordering needed |
| OK | Batches balanced across arms | Batch should still go in models as a covariate |
| OK | Counts whole, non-negative, no NAs, no failed RNAseq samples | Nothing |
| Watch | `B006` shallow microbiome sample (5,247 counts) | Consider excluding if it behaves oddly in ordinations |
| Watch | 86 / 220 species never observed | Pre-filter zero species before distance-based analyses |
| Watch | `B018`, `B029` have no cytokines | Drop those two rows in cytokine analyses only |
| Note | 24 genes lack a symbol | Helper already substitutes Ensembl IDs |

**How you could check me yourself:** the claims above are all one-liners. For
example, open `data/2-workshop2/group_b_contraception/02_microbiome_counts.csv`
in a spreadsheet and check that column B's header is `B001` while the metadata
file's second row also starts with `B001` — that's the order check by eye. Or
re-run the depth figure with a different cut-off: if I am wrong about `B006`
being the only shallow sample, the `shallow` table in section 3 will show more
rows than I reported.

## Choices made

- Loaded all six files through `R/count_tables.R::read_counts("group_b")` rather than reading each CSV by hand — the alternative was six separate `read_csv()` calls, which is more code to get wrong.
- Checked sample order with `identical()` (exact order, not just set equality) — the alternative was `setequal()`, which would pass even if the columns were shuffled, and shuffled columns are exactly the failure mode that silently corrupts DESeq2 results.
- Kept all 93 samples in the report — the alternative was dropping `B006`, `B018` and `B029` now, but QC should flag, not decide; each analysis document can drop what matters for it.
- Used raw (untransformed) counts for every check — the alternative was checking relative abundances, but normalisation is a later step and raw counts are where errors live.
- Used 10,000 counts as the "shallow" cut-off for flagging (not excluding) microbiome samples — the alternative cut-offs (1,000 or 5,000) would flag nothing here; the median is ~29,000 and only `B006` sits low.
- Judged batch balance and depth differences by eye (tables and plots) — the alternative was a formal test (e.g. a Kruskal–Wallis on depth by batch), overkill for 93 samples where the medians are close.
- Checked `bv` against the Nugent >= 7 cut-off — the alternative was trusting the label, but a label that disagrees with its source score is a classic QC catch.
- Treated the 15 cytokines as continuous measurements and only checked for negatives and failed assays — the alternative, distribution checks per cytokine, belongs in the cytokine analysis document where a transform would be chosen.
